title: Lost Learning
program_note:
Lost Learning, written for David Geringas and Jascha Nemstov, both celebrates and laments European Jewry, its culture, and its collective artistic expression and learning — much of which was lost or destroyed in the Holocaust — as well as the work of some of the greatest Jewish inventors.
The first movement begins as a lament, but then gets transformed into a dance — or more accurately the memory of one.  As the dance gets encrusted with memories it transforms back into a lament.
The second movement celebrates the discoveries of the French Nobel-prize winning inventor Gabriel Lippmann, in particular lenticular printing (which now, a century later, has become the core of virtual-reality 3D imaging), in which viewing a two-dimensional image from different angles results in different images or perspectives on the same image.  Here, the different angles of time result in two different musical “images” heard, one at the beginning, one at the end, and interleaved in the middle.
An interlude follows, honoring the Polish-born mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot (credited as the “father of fractals”), in which we hear the same lament that began the piece in ways that variously repeat and echo itself.
Lastly, Lithuanian Late-Night uses a Lithuanian klezmer tune from around the turn of the 20th century; after flowering from the memories of the previous movement it submerges back into the sense of loss with which the piece began.

Lost Learning is about 20 minutes total duration, with the individual movements approximately as shown:
1.  Lithuanian Lament 6:00
2.  Lippmann’s Lenticular 4:50
iii.  Interlude:  Mandelbrot’s Memory   3:00
1.  Lithuanian Late-Night 6:00

David S. Lefkowitz
Los Angeles, CA
26 June, 2017
